findings.title: An embodied scene of subjection
findings.claim: The focus's offenders, lowered heads, and presence before their Lord become a bodily scene of subjection; the following verses place that posture within a fixed judgment and punishment for prior deeds.
findings.mechanism: The offender term supplies a culpable group, the head and lowering words give that group a visible bodily orientation, and the presence construction meets the Lord as one who governs. The next two verses add a fixed sentence and punishment grounded in prior conduct. The body-mass branch contributes an image formed by the collective and its heads, rather than a second dictionary gloss for the offender word.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see social standing and bodily orientation together: the named offenders appear as a physical group made low before the one who governs the coming judgment.
findings.containment: The focus still names wrongdoers with their heads lowered before their Lord. The added body and rank image does not say that the people are literally upside down, assign a single motive to them, or explain each person's conduct.

epistemic.reason: The channel supports and accepted focus branches are trusted. The head branch has qualified lexical identity, and the collective body reading is an explicitly bounded contextual image.

findings.title: Recognition arrives with a closed return
findings.claim: Against believers who respond to reminders and act before seeing their hidden reward, the focus's speakers say they have seen and heard, ask to be sent back after death, and promise good work. The surrounding return and reward sequence makes their proposed repair a late plea, while leaving its stated words intact.
findings.mechanism: The sight and hearing carriers meet the believers' response to reminders in 32:15 and their unseen-reward sequence in 32:16–17; hearing's compliance facet and the focus's certainty then meet the deeds and abode in 32:19. The return request meets 32:11's death-and-return-to-the-Lord scene and 32:20's repeated failed exits. Together these context relations change the promised work from an abstract future possibility into action requested after the pericope has already shown both timely response and closed return.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hear the focus's certainty as recognition that has arrived after the point when it could guide action: elsewhere in the same sequence, response and effort precede the sight of reward.
findings.containment: The focus still says that the speakers saw and heard, ask to be sent back, promise good deeds, and assert certainty. This comparison does not declare their plea insincere or identify the faithful and the speakers as the same people; the return-after-death image is bounded by the supplied pericope.

epistemic.reason: The channel supports and connection text are trusted. Exact Arabic for 32:15–17 is supplied, but its context-word indices and root assignments come from a legacy-unbound HFT trace and remain attributed.

findings.title: A fixed record meets a future promise
findings.claim: The immediate continuation can be read as answering the speakers' promise of future work with a fixed sentence, reciprocal neglect, experienced punishment, and deeds already on record; the promise does not by itself reopen the opportunity they request.
findings.mechanism: The focus asks to be returned so its speakers can act. In 32:13 the trace attributes a fixed due and a completed filling to the announced sentence; in 32:14 it attributes reciprocal forgetting, tasting, and prior work as the grounds of punishment. Those carriers meet the focus's hypothetical future agency, changing the neighboring sequence into an answer-like contrast between proposed intention and completed conduct.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can keep the plea audible as a request for a second chance while seeing why the immediate continuation treats the past record as decisive.
findings.containment: The focus still voices a promise that may be sincere. The answer-like relation is an attributed contextual reading; the alternative that the verses give a general collective explanation rather than a direct reply to each speaker remains live.

epistemic.reason: All cited HFT anchors have exact supplied Arabic and are within 32:11–20, but the HFT identity is legacy_unbound, its source packet is broader than the pericope, and context morphology and root joins are not independently supplied.

findings.title: Chosen response and coerced lowering
findings.claim: The focus's lowered heads and request to act follow sight, while the faithful in 32:15–17 answer reminder with chosen prostration and bodily effort before seeing their hidden reward; the postures form a temporally reversed contrast.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries sight before lowered heads and a future-work plea. The adjacent 32:15–17 sequence, as traced, moves from reminder to willing fall and prostration, from rest to effort, and then to a reward not yet seen. Those context roles meet the focus's posture, seeing, and promised action. The relation makes the lowered heads a coerced counterpart to a response already enacted willingly.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see posture carrying both agency and timing: one group acts when reminded and before seeing reward; the focus's speakers see and then ask to begin.
findings.containment: The focus still depicts lowered heads and the speakers' appeal, and the context still depicts prostration and effort. The comparison does not establish that the groups are identical or that they share a single motive; the HFT's alternative that both sequences share only a broad submission image remains possible.

epistemic.reason: The Arabic anchors for 32:15–17 are exact and complete, but their word indices, root assignments, and attributed roles come from a legacy-unbound trace without independent target morphology.
